reasoning.Student A:
My stated preferences are w > y > x > z. My priorities are: w: 1, x: 2, y: 1, z: 2. Most applicants favor y > x > w > z.

Since I am risk-averse, I want to maximize my chances of getting into my top choices. I have top priority at both w and y. Given that most applicants favor y > x > w > z, it is likely that y will be more competitive than w.

If I rank w first, I am guaranteed to get into w because I have the highest priority. This eliminates any uncertainty. If I rank y first, I might get y (which I prefer to x), but there's a chance I might not get y due to other applicants with high priority. I would then be at the mercy of x and z, where I have only priority 2.

Therefore, to minimize risk and guarantee my best possible outcome, I should rank w first. After that, I should rank y, since I still prefer it to x and z. I rank x next, and z last.
